job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (as amended October 6, 2026)

This review is based only on the text provided. I did not have the pre-amendment text, so I could not confirm which provisions the manager's amendment changed.

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 10,000-ton threshold applies "by a single vessel," so an operation split across several vessels, each below the threshold, falls outside the definition. The text also doesn't say whether the threshold is measured wet or dry, or how tonnage is aggregated across an operation.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "Other mineral resources" is undefined, and the definition covers only "recovery." Processing, sediment discharge, and tailings disposal are not addressed, so activities with significant impacts can escape unless the Secretary designates them under subparagraph (B).

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 200-meter depth floor is not tied to any defined scope for "seabed." Shallower seabed extraction is excluded entirely, and the bill does not address overlap with existing federal leasing authority, such as the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (verify).

4. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** The "Secretary" is never identified; Sec. 6 refers to the Secretary of State, which suggests the drafters may have meant a different official. The subparagraph also gives no criteria for "comparable" risk, no procedure or notice, no deadline, and no judicial review standard, and "deep-sea ecosystems" is undefined. A discretionary designation like this is easy to challenge in either direction.

5. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers only citizens and state-organized corporations. It does not clearly cover LLCs, partnerships, or trusts, which are common in mining ventures, and "State" is not defined to address D.C. or the territories.

6. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel":** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold removes smaller vessels from the registry and reporting requirements. "Equipped for" is ambiguous (capable of recovery, or actually used for it), and "vessel" is undefined, so platforms, remotely operated vehicles, and non-self-propelled collectors may escape.

## Prohibition (Sec. 3)

7. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in":** The phrase is undefined and does not reach financing, equipment supply, processing, sale, transport, or import of minerals mined abroad. Material recovered overseas could enter U.S. commerce without any violation.

8. **Sec. 3(a), "person" and "in the United States":** Neither term is defined, and the bill doesn't say whether "in the United States" covers territorial waters, the Exclusive Economic Zone, the outer continental shelf, or the high seas. Foreign persons operating outside U.S. jurisdiction appear to be untouched, which matters for coordination with the International Seabed Authority.

9. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license":** The term is undefined and not cross-referenced to any licensing regime. The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act is likely relevant, but it isn't cited (verify). Exploration licenses typically don't authorize commercial recovery, so it's unclear what "mining conducted under" such a license means.

10. **Sec. 3(b), scope of exemption:** The exemption has no tonnage cap, area limit, or sunset, and it doesn't require that the license still be valid. It also doesn't address renewals, amendments, or transfers of pre-enactment licenses, so a grandfathered operation could expand indefinitely.

11. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment":** This is the bill's largest gap. "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no plan requirement, permit, tonnage cap, duration limit, reporting requirement, or scientific-purpose test. Commercial-scale recovery could be labeled as assessment, and the bill doesn't prohibit selling the material.

## Registry and Reporting (Sec. 4)

12. **Sec. 4(a), "operator" and deadlines:** "Operator" is undefined, and there is no deadline for registration. An operator who never registers a vessel is not clearly in violation of any deadline.

13. **Sec. 4(b), report contents:** The bill does not specify what the quarterly report must contain, such as tonnage, location, depth, or discharge data. As written, the reports cannot verify the 10,000-ton threshold or support any finding that a Sec. 3(c) activity is actually an assessment. The bill also has no deadline per quarter, no public-disclosure requirement, no audit power, and no specific false-statement penalty.

14. **Sec. 4 versus Sec. 5, no penalty:** Sec. 5 penalties attach only to violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register a vessel or file a report carries no stated penalty. This is the most significant enforcement gap in the registry provisions.

## Penalties (Sec. 5)

15. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement mechanism:** The bill does not name an enforcing agency, grant civil enforcement authority, set an administrative or judicial procedure, or authorize injunctions. It also has no forfeiture provision for vessels, equipment, or minerals.

16. **Sec. 5(a), date conflict with Sec. 8:** The civil penalty applies to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 3 does not take effect until 180 days later under Sec. 8. Either the language is meaningless, or the drafters intended the prohibition to take effect at enactment, and the two sections need to be reconciled.

17. **Sec. 5(a), penalty unit and limitations:** The "day" in the per-day penalty is not defined. It is unclear whether the penalty runs per vessel, per operation, or per violation. The bill also does not address inflation adjustment or the statute of limitations, which default to general federal rules (verify).

18. **Sec. 5(b), criminal provisions:** "Willfully" is undefined, and the criminal provision does not address corporate officer liability, attempt, or conspiracy. Application to conduct on the high seas also depends on general jurisdictional principles that the bill does not state.

## International Agreement (Sec. 6)

19. **Sec. 6, "shall seek to negotiate":** The provision imposes no obligation to conclude an agreement and no duty to report to Congress. It is also unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to starting negotiations or to concluding them, and "equivalent" prohibitions is undefined.

20. **Sec. 6, effect of an agreement:** The bill does not say what happens to Sec. 3 if an agreement is concluded, and it does not reference the International Seabed Authority, which may be central to any such agreement.

## Duration and Sunset (Sec. 7)

21. **Sec. 7(a), "serious harm" and the NASEM process:** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill does not say whom or what it protects. It also doesn't require the National Academies to produce a report, sets no deadline, and provides no funding.

22. **Sec. 7(a), joint resolution path:** The provision says Congress "finds by joint resolution," but it doesn't say whether the resolution goes to the President for signature or veto. That ambiguity affects whether the mechanism can actually be used.

23. **Sec. 7(a) versus Sec. 7(b), direct conflict:** Sec. 7(a) keeps the prohibition in force until a joint resolution is adopted, but Sec. 7(b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect 10 years after enactment. The bill does not say whether Sec. 3 survives the sunset in any circumstance, and a court would have to reconcile the two provisions.

24. **Sec. 7(b), sunset timing and savings:** The 10 years run from enactment, not from the Sec. 8 effective date, so the prohibition would be in force for only about 9.5 years. The bill has no savings clause to preserve liability for pre-sunset violations, and it doesn't say whether the Sec. 3(b) and 3(c) exemptions or the registry obligations end with the Act.

## Effective Date (Sec. 8)

25. **Sec. 8, 180-day window:** The bill has no transition or anti-rush provision. Operators could recover minerals during the six months before the prohibition takes effect, and because Sec. 4 also begins on the effective date, that period is unmonitored. The bill does not address operations that begin between enactment and the effective date.

## Structural Issues

26. **Undefined terms and missing general provisions:** Beyond the terms noted above, "seabed mineral resources," "vessel," "operator," and "deep-sea ecosystems" are all undefined. The bill also lacks a findings or purpose section (which courts use to interpret ambiguous text), a grant of rulemaking authority, an appropriations provision, a judicial review provision, and a severability clause. Each makes implementation harder or leaves the bill more exposed to a legal challenge.

## Priorities for Markup Coverage

If space is limited, these items are the most consequential:
- **Item 23** (Sec. 7(a) versus 7(b) conflict)
- **Items 10–11** (Sec. 3(b) and 3(c) exemptions)
- **Item 14** (no penalty for registry violations)
- **Item 16** (date conflict between Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8)
- **Item 1** (per-vessel threshold)
- **Item 7** (foreign-mined material)

## Notes for Staff

- **Verify statutory cross-references.** Items 3, 9, 17, and the discussion of Sec. 3(b) mention statutes and rules that I could not check, including the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, and federal civil-penalty and limitations provisions. My knowledge has a June 2026 cutoff, so confirm current law with CRS or the committee.
- **Compare against the prior text.** Run a redline of the October 6 manager's amendment before publishing. Section 3(c) and the Sec. 7 language may have changed in that amendment, and our coverage should describe those changes accurately.
- **Framing.** These are drafting observations about enforceability and clarity, not positions on the bill. Phrasing like "the bill does not specify" or "this could be read to" will keep the coverage consistent with our nonpartisan standard.
